title: How solar PV panels are mounted and fixed to a roof
subtitle: Understanding the racking system, roof penetration, and what the installer does on your roof
excerpt: Solar PV panels are fixed to the roof via a racking system of rails and hooks rather than directly to the tiles. The hooks anchor into the rafters and penetrate the felt underlay with a flashing seal. This guide explains what the installer does, how to check the work, and what questions to ask.
sourceNotes: MCS 012 installation standard for solar PV systems (2023 edition). LABC guidance on structural checking for roof PV loads. BS EN 1991-1-4 for wind load calculation relevant to roof-mounted systems. Racking manufacturer technical guides (generic hookless vs hook-mounted systems).

glossaryTerms.definition: Photovoltaic panels that convert sunlight directly into electricity. Output is measured in watts-peak (Wp) under standard test conditions.

content.text: Solar PV panels are not attached directly to tiles. They sit on a system of aluminium rails that span several rafters, held down by hooks that fasten through the tile into the rafter timber below. The rails carry the panels; the hooks carry the load. A 4 kWp array of 10 to 12 panels weighs around 150 to 250 kg, distributed over 20 to 30 m² of roof.
The racking system: how it works
Most UK residential
solar PV

installations use a hook-and-rail system. The installer locates each rafter by probing through the tile (or using a rafter finder from inside the loft) and marks the spacing. Hooks are inserted under the tile above each rafter, bedded on a rubber compressible seal, and screwed into the rafter with a 6 to 8 mm stainless steel structural screw. The tile sits back down over the hook.
Horizontal rails are clipped onto the hooks at a spacing matched to the panel frame holes, typically 800 to 1,000 mm apart.
The panels clip onto the rails with end clamps and mid-clamps. No drilling through the panel frame is required for most standard formats.
DC cables from each panel run under the rail along the roof to a cable entry point at the roof-to-wall junction, where they enter the loft.
The roof penetration and waterproofing

Each hook requires a small slot cut in the roofing felt underlay for the hook stem to pass through. The compressible rubber pad on the hook base seals against the underlay. A lead or EPDM flashing is fitted to the upper tile where the hook seat sits, directing water around the hook and down the tile surface.

DC cables enter the loft through a grommet in the underlay at the eaves or through a tile duct specifically designed for solar cable entry. The grommet or duct must be self-sealing and not allow rainwater ingress.
What to check after installation
Inspect the loft underlay from inside within a week of installation. Look for daylight around hook stems, tears in the underlay, or pooling water below the cable grommet.
Check tiles: no cracked tiles from the installation and no tiles sitting above their neighbours where hooks have been inserted.
Check the MCS certificate lists the racking specification (rail and hook models) and confirms a structural rafter check.
What the
inverter
connection looks like
DC cables from the roof run into the inverter, typically wall-mounted in the loft or utility room. The inverter connects to the AC consumer unit via a dedicated circuit. The
MCS
certificate records the inverter model, the array size, and the G98 or G99 grid connection notification.
Troubleshooter

rows.symptom: Drip appears in loft below the panel area after rain
rows.cause: Cable entry grommet not fully seated, or hook flashing not fully bedded on the tile above
rows.fix: Contact the installer immediately and request a roof inspection. This is a warranty issue; do not attempt repair yourself on an energised solar roof.

rows.symptom: A row of tiles is visibly lifted above the surrounding surface after installation
rows.cause: Hook has been set too high, or tile is sitting on the hook shank rather than the hook seat
rows.fix: Ask the installer to re-seat the affected hooks; a lifted tile can allow wind-driven water entry over the years.
